explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then…” (Galatians 5:1). The freedom is already handed over, so the job now is to hold your ground. I dig in on my gold base when somebody tries to shove me around, and that's the picture.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: Close, but the freedom is already theirs. Paul says Christ has set them free, and that's a gift, not a paycheck. Nobody punches a clock for a gift, friend. What Paul asks for is standing firm (Galatians 5:1).

Paul never says to hush up. He says, “Stand firm, then…” (Galatians 5:1), and he's pretty loud himself in this letter. Standing firm and tiptoeing around are two different things. I think a freedom you're holding onto doesn't need to hide.

True. Paul says not to be “encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1). A yoke is a heavy load strapped on you, and that's the one he doesn't want them picking back up. Notice the words “once more.” He's warning about a load that's out there waiting for them.

Paul really does say this. The verse reads, “…do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1). He gives the warning right after saying Christ has set them free. So the card is true, and the warning is right there in the text.

No value at all. Paul says if they let themselves be circumcised, “Christ will be of no value to you at all” (Galatians 5:2). There's no half credit and no discount there. He means every word, and he put his own name on it.

Ha, that's the opposite of what Paul says. He says Christ “will be of no value to you at all” if they go that route (Galatians 5:2). It's not a bonus round, friend. It's a warning, and he signs it with his own name.

You'd think nothing changes, but Paul says it does. He says Christ “will be of no value to you at all” (Galatians 5:2). That isn't staying the same, and it isn't even a small drop. It's all the way down, and Paul wanted them to know it.

Not quite, because Paul says more than one command. He says the man who gets himself circumcised “is obligated to obey the whole law” (Galatians 5:3). The word is whole, friend. It's a package deal, and there's no picking one item off the shelf.

False, and you read it right. Paul says, “Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law” (Galatians 5:3). One command is not the deal, the whole law is. Paul testifies to this, and I'd listen.

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. “You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ” (Galatians 5:4). Severed means cut off, and Paul chose that word on purpose. He says it plain, and it's a heavy line.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: You'd think so, but Paul says the opposite. Those trying to be justified by the law “have been severed from Christ” (Galatians 5:4). Severed is cut off, not brought near. I think that's why he's so serious in these lines.

Paul says the reverse. He says they “have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4). Trying to earn it doesn't stack grace up, and it doesn't work like a rewards card. Grace is not something you earn extra of.

Faith is the word. “But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness” (Galatians 5:5). Faith is how they wait, and the Spirit is who they wait through. Paul puts both in one short line.

That's the very thing Paul just warned about. Anyone trying to be justified by the law has been severed from Christ (Galatians 5:4). Then he turns and says, “But by faith…” (Galatians 5:5). That little “But” is doing a lot of work.

Effort sounds right to a lot of us, I'll give you that. But Paul's line says, “But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit…” (Galatians 5:5). Effort isn't the word in that verse. The word is faith, and the waiting happens through the Spirit.

That's it. “What matters is faith expressing itself through love” (Galatians 5:6). Faith isn't just something you hold in your head. It shows up in how you love people. Paul says it right after saying neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value.

Paul goes the other direction here. A man who gets circumcised is “obligated to obey the whole law” (Galatians 5:3), and he says that's not where the weight lands. What matters, he says, is “faith expressing itself through love” (Galatians 5:6). A perfect score isn't the answer.

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention a family line in this verse. He says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, then lands on “faith expressing itself through love” (Galatians 5:6). That's what matters in Christ Jesus. Faith and love are the answer.
Paul says the opposite. “Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you” (Galatians 5:8). Whatever is slowing them down, it isn't coming from the One who calls them. So the answer is false.
False, and that's what the text says. “Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you” (Galatians 5:8). Paul says it short and clear. The One who calls them is not behind that persuasion.

The whole batch, just like he says. “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (Galatians 5:9). Little goes in, and it reaches all of it. Any baker will tell you that dough doesn't keep secrets.
I get why you'd think so, but Paul says more than that. “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (Galatians 5:9). It doesn't stay on top. The word is whole.

Paul says it reaches further than one spot. “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (Galatians 5:9). A little goes in, and it works through all of it. That's the point of the picture.

Yes. Paul says, “The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians 5:10). Whoever he may be, so Paul doesn't name him. That's a serious line, so I'll just let it stand.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. “The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians 5:10). He doesn't get let off. It's a heavy line, and Paul doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Nope, Paul says nothing about promotions here. He says, “The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians 5:10). The one troubling them faces judgment. That's a serious thing to say.

Not quite. Paul is asking an “if” question: “if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (Galatians 5:11). His question shows he isn't preaching it, or the persecution wouldn't make sense. He's making a point, not confessing.

False. Paul asks, “if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” (Galatians 5:11). His question points the other way. He isn't preaching it, and he adds that otherwise “the offense of the cross has been abolished.”

True. “For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5:13). Freedom is the gift, and Paul adds a warning right with it. He's glad they're free, and he doesn't want them to waste it.
Paul does give that warning. He says, “…do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5:13). It comes right after he says they were called to freedom. So the card is true.
That's the one. “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Galatians 5:14). One decree holds the whole thing. That's a lot packed into a short line, friend.

That's one of the commands in the law (Exodus 20:8), but it's not the one Paul picks here. He says, “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Galatians 5:14). That's his single decree.

That's a command in the law too (Exodus 20:12), but Paul doesn't pick it here. He says, “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Galatians 5:14). Neighbor love is the one he names.

Consumed is the word. “But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15). Biting and devouring is how it starts, and consumed is where it ends. Paul says to watch out.

Scattered sounds believable, but it isn't Paul's word. He says, “…watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15). Consumed fits with the biting and devouring just before it. It's a serious warning.

Shamed is a good guess, but Paul says something stronger. “…watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15). Biting and devouring leads to being consumed, friend. That's why he says to watch out.
